opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question, and I want to be careful not to overstate the analogy, because the brain wasn't designed so much as shaped by evolutionary pressures that don't necessarily apply to the systems we're building.

That said, I think there are a few useful lessons. If you look at primates, and humans especially, a huge fraction of cortex is devoted to vision. That's not arbitrary. Vision gives you dense, high-bandwidth information about the world at a distance, and it's very good for planning and for understanding objects and their relationships. So one lesson is that the brain invests most heavily in the modality that carries the most useful structure for the problems the organism actually has to solve.

For AI, that suggests we should ask what the high-value modality is for a given task, rather than assume text is the answer for everything. Language models have been remarkably successful partly because text is a compressed, abstracted form of human knowledge. But for robotics or anything that needs physical intuition, I'd bet heavily on vision and proprioception, and maybe touch, carrying much more of the load.

The second lesson is less about which modality wins and more about integration. The brain doesn't keep its senses in separate silos. There's cross-modal prediction everywhere. You hear something and your visual system is already anticipating what it'll see. Multisensory areas use one modality to supervise another. I think that's underexploited in AI. We often bolt modalities together late in the pipeline, when the brain suggests you'd get richer representations from having them constantly predicting and correcting each other.

The third thing, and I say this as someone who spends a lot of time on behavior and movement, is that the brain's sensory biases are ultimately in service of action. Perception exists to help you move through the world and do things. So if we want systems that are grounded and robust, we should probably care less about passive perception benchmarks and more about whether the representations support good decisions and control.

So, in short: don't copy the brain's specific ratios blindly, but take seriously the principle that you allocate capacity to whatever modality carries the most actionable structure, and that you let modalities teach each other.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the first thing to say is that the brain's bias isn't really a bias toward vision or audition per se, it's a bias toward whatever modality gives you the most reliable, low-latency information about what matters for survival. For primates that happens to be vision, and you see it in the sheer amount of cortex devoted to it. But for a bat it's echolocation, for a rat it's whiskers and smell. The point is that evolution allocates representational capacity according to where the useful signal is, and I think that's the real lesson for AI, not "copy the primate sensory hierarchy."

The second thing, and this comes from my background working on neural data and animal behavior, is that the brain doesn't treat modalities as separate problems that get fused at the end. There's cross-talk very early. Multisensory integration happens in regions people used to think were purely visual or purely auditory. So when we build these systems with a vision encoder and a text encoder that only meet at some late projection layer, that's actually a pretty unnatural architecture. The brain's version is more like, information from one modality is constantly reshaping how you interpret the other, and that happens throughout the hierarchy.

And then the third piece is about what's actually being prioritized. Language models are, in a sense, built on the single modality that's most compressed and most human-curated. Text is this incredibly dense distillation of what humans thought was worth writing down. That's why it works so well. But the brain's heavy investment in vision and proprioception is telling us something about grounding. Those modalities are where you learn the structure of physical reality: object permanence, causality, what happens when you push on things. I think the systems that end up being robust in the world are going to need something closer to that, where the "expensive" modalities aren't an afterthought bolted onto a language model but are the thing the representation is actually built on.

So if I had to summarize: don't copy the brain's specific allocation, but take seriously the principle that representational budget should follow informational value, that integration should happen early and throughout, and that the modalities the brain spends the most on are probably the ones we're currently underinvesting in.

astra-6.text:
I think the interesting question is which biases are useful for learning, and which are just consequences of the particular problems our brains evolved to solve. We rely heavily on vision, but that doesn’t necessarily mean vision should play the same role in every AI system.

What seems more generalizable is that our senses give us different views of the same world. You see something fall, you hear it hit the floor, and you can reach out and pick it up. Those signals constrain one another. That gives you a way to learn structure without somebody explicitly labeling every experience.

So I’d take the brain as a source of hypotheses about useful inductive biases, rather than a blueprint. Build systems that can connect information across modalities, but choose their biases based on what they need to do. And then test whether those biases actually improve learning and generalization.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it should make us question the assumption that every modality ought to be treated the same way. In the brain, different senses have different jobs, and we rely on them differently depending on the situation. Vision is useful for some things; touch or hearing may be much more informative for others.

For AI, the interesting question is whether those biases are useful constraints. If you’re building a system that interacts with the physical world, maybe it should have some structure that reflects how its sensors work and what actions it can take. But I wouldn’t assume that copying the brain’s particular balance is always the right answer. Our sensory systems reflect our evolutionary history. An AI might have very different sensors and very different tasks.

So I’d take the principle seriously—that intelligence develops through particular ways of accessing the world—without treating the human arrangement as the only possible blueprint.
